Who was Søren Kierkegaard?
Danish philosopher (1813–1855). The human right and duty to choose – the book 'Either/Or' (Enten-eller, 1843).
Who was Carl Nielsen?
Composer (1865–1931). The symphony 'The Inextinguishable' (Det uudslukkelige, 1916) and melodies for songs such as 'Jens Vejmand' and 'Solen er så rød, mor'.
Who was Karen Blixen, and what did she write?
Author (1885–1962). Owned a coffee farm in Kenya – 'Out of Africa' (Den afrikanske farm, 1937). Also 'Seven Gothic Tales' (Syv fantastiske fortællinger, 1935).
Who was Tove Ditlevsen?
Author (1917–76), grew up in a poor family in Vesterbro. 'Barndommens Gade' (Childhood Street, 1943), 'Childhood' and 'Youth' (1967), 'Dependency' (Gift, 1971).
Who was Arne Jacobsen?
Architect (1902–1971), known for functionalism. The furniture 'Series 7' (7-eren) and 'the Egg'. Designed the National Bank in Copenhagen.
Which films has Thomas Vinterberg made?
'The Celebration' (Festen, 1998), 'The Hunt' (Jagten, 2012), 'The Commune' (Kollektivet, 2016) and 'Another Round' (Druk, 2020, Oscar in 2021).
Which film did Susanne Bier win an Oscar for?
'In a Better World' (Hævnen, 2010).
When has Denmark won the Eurovision Song Contest, and with whom?
1963: Grethe and Jørgen Ingmann ('Dansevise'). 2000: the Olsen Brothers. 2013: Emmelie de Forest ('Only Teardrops').
Which group is known for 'Barbie Girl'?
Aqua (Danish-Norwegian) – sold 28 million CDs.
Who is Olafur Eliasson, and what is 'Your rainbow panorama'?
Danish-Icelandic artist (born 1967). A 150 m long circular glass walkway on top of ARoS in Aarhus (2011).
Who was Yahya Hassan?
Author (1995–2020). Debuted in 2013 with the poetry collection 'Yahya Hassan' – the best-selling one in Denmark (over 100,000). Sparked debate about young immigrants in ghetto areas.
What is fastelavn (Shrovetide)?
Carnival – children dress up and 'hit the cat out of the barrel'. Whoever knocks off the last board becomes 'cat king'. Seven weeks before Easter.
What does Easter mark?
That Jesus was crucified, died and rose from the dead.
Which days are the Easter holidays?
Palm Sunday, Maundy Thursday, Good Friday, Easter Sunday and Easter Monday. Easter falls in March or April (not on fixed dates).
What do people often drink at an Easter lunch?
Påskebryg (a special Easter beer). People also give Easter eggs.
When is Pentecost (pinse), and what is remembered?
Seven weeks after Easter (May/June). In memory of the Holy Spirit coming down to earth. Whit Sunday and Whit Monday are public holidays.
What is celebrated on 1 May?
The workers' international day of demonstration and celebration (since 1889).
What is celebrated on 5 May?
Denmark's liberation in 1945 – many people put candles in their windows.
What is celebrated on 5 June (Constitution Day)?
The Constitution of 1849. Constitution Day meetings with speeches about democracy. Not an official day off, but many offices and shops close.
What happens on Midsummer Eve (sankthansaften, 23 June)?
Bonfires are lit – marking midsummer. A mix of pagan tradition and Christianity.
Which days are holidays at Christmas?
24, 25 and 26 December (Christmas Eve, Christmas Day and Boxing Day).
What happens on Christmas Eve?
Christmas church service, Christmas tree, Christmas dinner, dancing around the tree, Christmas hymns and presents.
What is a julefrokost (Christmas lunch)?
A lunch in December (and on Christmas Day/Boxing Day) with lots of food, beer and snaps.
How is New Year celebrated?
On 31 December with parties and fireworks. The King's New Year speech at 18:00. The prime minister's New Year speech on 1 January.
What are Ramadan and Eid al-Fitr?
Ramadan: the Muslim month of fasting (in memory of Muhammad's first revelation). Eid al-Fitr: the celebration when Ramadan ends.
What is remembered at Jewish Passover and Jewish Pentecost (Shavuot)?
Passover: the Jews' exodus from Egypt (lamb and unleavened bread). Shavuot: the covenant at Mount Sinai (Moses and the Ten Commandments).
What is Chinese New Year?
A Chinese holiday – starts on the first day of the first month and ends with the Lantern Festival on the 15th day.
Which other special days are mentioned?
Halloween (American – dressing up) and carnival on the South American model (samba music, parades).
When did Denmark join the UN and NATO?
What did Denmark do from World War II until about 1990?
Took part in many UN peacekeeping missions.
What is an 'activist foreign policy'?
After the Cold War (about 1990) Denmark took a more active part in international conflicts – not only peacekeeping missions.
What happened in the Gulf War of 1990–91?
Iraq occupied Kuwait. The USA led a military operation with a UN resolution. Denmark sent a ship that did not take part in fighting.
Where did Danish soldiers see combat in the 1990s?
Bosnia (1994, as part of UN forces). Kosovo 1999: Danish fighter jets took part in NATO's operation.
What happened on 11 September 2001?
Terrorist attacks on the USA – about 3,000 killed. Gave NATO a new focus on fighting terror.
Why did NATO-led forces invade Afghanistan in October 2001?
Al Qaeda was behind 9/11 and had a base there. The Taliban government was removed.
Where were the Danish soldiers in Afghanistan, and how many were killed?
Helmand province. 44 Danish soldiers lost their lives. The Taliban took power again in 2021.
Why did the USA go to war against Iraq in 2003?
Iraq did not cooperate on disarmament, and the USA believed Iraq had weapons of mass destruction. None were ever found. Saddam Hussein was removed.
What did Denmark take part in in 2011 and 2014?
2011: UN-mandated operation in Libya against Gaddafi (aircraft, bombing). 2014: US-led mission against Islamic State in Iraq and Syria (aircraft and training).
What have Russia's actions in 2014 and 2022 meant for NATO?
The occupation of Crimea (2014) and the war in Ukraine (since 2022) – NATO has returned to defending its own territory.
What was decided about defence and conscription in 2024?
More money for defence up to 2030, more soldiers – and conscription extended from four to 11 months.
Why was Greenland important during the Cold War?
It lies between the USA and the Soviet Union – the shortest flight and missile route passes over Greenland.
What did Denmark and the USA agree about Greenland in 1951?
An agreement on US military activities. The USA built the air base near Qaanaaq (Thule) – now Pituffik Space Base.
Why is the Arctic in focus?
The ice is melting – new opportunities for oil, gas, minerals and shorter shipping routes. The USA, Russia and China are interested.
What has Denmark decided in 2025 about Greenland?
To strengthen defence around Greenland with Arctic ships and drones. Donald Trump's wish for Greenland to become part of the USA has been rejected by the Greenlandic and Danish governments.
What is discrimination?
Treating people differently and worse because of e.g. religion, political views, skin colour, gender, ethnicity, sexual orientation or age.
What is illegal to say or write publicly?

Something that mocks or threatens others because of race, skin colour, religion or sexual orientation – as well as supporting or encouraging crimes (e.g. violence) or expressing support for a terrorist attack.
What is a hate crime?
A crime against, for example, a minority committed because of the victim's ethnic origin, religion, sexual orientation, etc. Can be punished especially severely.
How many hate crimes did the police register in 2022–24?
2,108 cases (about 702 a year – roughly two a day).
What were the most common reasons for hate crimes in 2022–24?
Race/ethnicity 48%, religion 36%, sexual orientation 21%.
What does 'freedom must be used responsibly' mean?
The state can limit freedom so that it is not used to harm others – for example to discriminate.
How many hate crimes were directed against Jews in 2022–24?
430 – even though only 6–8,000 Jews live in Denmark. Almost one in three religiously motivated hate crimes and one in five of all hate crimes.
What happened in Randers in 2019 and at the synagogue in Copenhagen in 2015?

Randers: over 80 gravestones in a Jewish cemetery knocked over by neo-Nazis (9 November – Kristallnacht). 2015: terrorist attack at the synagogue, a Jewish guard was killed; the same day a film director was killed at Krudttønden.
What happened in the Folketing in 2003?

Two men attacked Prime Minister Anders Fogh Rasmussen and Foreign Minister Per Stig Møller with paint (protest against the Iraq war). Sentenced to three and four months in prison – it is especially serious to attack representatives of democracy.
Who protects threatened politicians?
The Danish Security and Intelligence Service (PET) – with bodyguards.
What is the greenhouse effect?
Greenhouse gases (e.g. CO2) let the sun's rays in but limit how much heat escapes – the temperature rises (global warming).
What has led to large CO2 emissions?
Burning fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) in production and transport.
How much has the temperature risen since 1850–1900?
More than one degree. The UN predicts 1.4–4.4 degrees warmer by the end of the century.
What is the Paris Agreement?
An agreement from 2015 in which almost all countries promise to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
How much did Denmark's emissions fall from 1990 to 2024?
About 53 percent.
What is the Danish Council on Climate Change (Klimarådet)?
Set up in 2014. Advises on and assesses the government's climate policy.
What does the 2019 Climate Act say?
Reduce emissions by 70% by 2030 (compared with 1990) and be climate neutral by 2050 at the latest.
What does climate neutral mean?
That you do not emit more greenhouse gases than you absorb.
What is the green transition?
Stopping using 'black' energy sources (oil and gas) and using renewable, green sources (sun, wind, hydropower).
What is Vindeby?
The world's first offshore wind farm (1991), off Lolland. Denmark has had wind turbines on land since the 1970s.
What share of Denmark's electricity consumption did wind turbines cover in 2025?
52 percent.
What share of energy consumption did renewable energy cover in 2025 vs. 1990?
50 percent in 2025 compared with 6 percent in 1990.
What are the energy islands, and where will they be?
Two islands to collect and convert energy from offshore wind turbines. One near Bornholm, one in the North Sea about 80 km off Jutland's west coast. To be built in the 2030s.
In which area has Denmark not yet seriously reduced emissions?
Transport – more electric cars are needed.
What does the state support homeowners in doing?
Replacing oil and gas boilers with heat pumps (a more climate-friendly home).
What is the Green Tripartite (Den Grønne Trepart)?
Cooperation between the government, municipalities, trade unions, environmental and business organisations. A 2024 plan for more nature, cleaner water and transforming agriculture.
How much of Denmark's area is farmland, and what has been agreed about nature?
60 percent. About 15% of farmland is to become nature (forest, bogs, streams).
What is special about Denmark's CO2 tax on agriculture?
The first country in the world with a direct tax on agriculture's emissions (cows, pigs, sheep, chickens).
